scenes.title: Cold open
narration: The Rhythms of the Brahmaputra
This is Assamese folk dance. 17th century to present.
on_screen: Title card: Assamese folk dance · India · 17th century to present

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Assamese folk dances have evolved from diverse tribal and religious roots.
The Bihu dance has records dating to 1694 under King Rudra Singha.
Sattriya was recognized as a classical dance in 2000.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Most tribal festivals occur in spring to celebrate cultivation or harvest.
Bihu welcomes the Assamese New Year.
Deodhani is used to appease goddesses.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Technique varies by style.
Bihu involves gender-specific lines, hip and wrist movements, and squats.
Jhumur involves holding waists and moving synchronously.
Watch for Bihu Twirls, Bhortal Cymbal Patterns.
on_screen: Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Lines and circles; gender-based separation.
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Instruments include the dhol (drum), mohor xingor pepa (horn), taal (cymbals), gogona (reed), toka (clapper), xutuli (whistle), serja (bowed), sifung (flute), tharkha (bamboo), and mandal.
Listen for the dhol, mohor xingor pepa, taal, gogona.
A blend of rhythmic percussion from the dhol and mandal, punctuated by the plaintive, high-pitched notes of the pepa or flute, and the metallic clatter of cymbals.
on_screen: Instrument names on screen as each is mentioned
Waveform or rhythm-pattern graphic: Formal rhythmic compositions called seus in Bihu; fast beat in Bhortal.
scenes.music: the music brief's underscore at its own tempo; drop narration under the hook of a verified recording if licensed, else original

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Costumes vary by tribe, such as the Bodo women's colourful dokhna and aronai.
Performers of Ojapali wear a pag-jama or ghuri, bangles, and a tangali.
Settings include open fields (Bihu), Satras (Sattriya/Jhumura), and temples (Devadasi).
on_screen: Image gallery: 3 licensed images with attribution
Reconstruction imagery allowed only from the costume notes, labelled 'reconstruction'

scenes.title: The people
narration: Narahari Burha Bhakat (Bhortal), King Rudra Singha (Bihu patron), Madhavdeva (Jhumura plays), Srimanta Sankardeva (Thiyo Naam).
Deori Bihu, Mising Bihu, Rati Bihu (Morans), and various types of Jhumura like Ramadani and Mela Nach.
Derived from tribal traditions, Satra monastic practices, and ancient Shakti religious rituals.
on_screen: Names on screen as they are spoken
Variant names as a small list

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Assamese folk dance is variant of Sattriya: A classical dance form derived from the Satra monastic tradition.
Assamese folk dance is parent of Thiyo Naam: Bhortal dance is derived from the Thiyo Naam tradition.
on_screen: Graph: the connections with their relation labels

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: Deodhani and Devadasi are ritualistic and sacred; outsiders should observe with respect and avoid participation unless invited by the community.

scenes.title: Until next time
narration: Explore the vibrant folk traditions of Assam, from the spring-time energy of Bihu to the ancient rituals of the Satras.
